title: Choreography and Motion Mapping
answer: Kinematic generation, notation, motion capture retargeting, crowd simulation and biomechanics.

children.name: Kinematic Video and Generated Movement
children.blurb: Kinematic video and generated movement covers work in which a body's motion is captured, modelled or synthesised, then used as the raw material for a finished moving image.

children.name: Dance Notation and Transcription
children.blurb: Dance notation and transcription covers the systems used to record human movement so that a dance can be restaged, analysed or preserved without the original dancers present.

children.name: Motion Capture and Retargeting
children.blurb: Motion capture and retargeting covers the pipeline that turns a performer's movement into a digital skeleton and then maps that skeleton onto a different character, rig, or body.

children.name: Crowd and Ensemble Simulation
children.blurb: Crowd and ensemble simulation covers the generation and control of many moving bodies at once, from stadium crowds and street scenes to corps de ballet and marching formations.

children.name: Biomechanical Analysis
children.blurb: Biomechanical analysis in choreography and motion mapping is the study of how a body actually moves, measured rather than guessed, and then turned into data a director, animator or choreographer can work with.

sections.body: Choreography and motion mapping is the use of artificial intelligence to generate, record, translate and analyse human movement. In practice, systems now produce short kinematic sequences from text or music prompts, track dancers through video, and retarget motion capture data from one body or rig to another. Choreographers use these tools to sketch phrases before rehearsal, while studios use them to previsualise staging and camera paths. Biomechanics researchers apply similar models to gait, balance and load, and crowd simulators fill stadiums and streets with agents that move plausibly rather than identically. The work sits between animation, dance and engineering, and it treats movement as data that can be measured, edited and recombined.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Generation of short, plausible movement is largely solved for screen and stage previsualisation, and marker based motion capture remains reliable in controlled spaces. What is not solved is long form coherence, contact, weight and intent, so generated phrases often drift, slide or lose the through line a choreographer would keep. Retargeting still struggles when proportions differ greatly or when a movement depends on balance and floor contact. Notation systems capture some dances well and resist others, and automated transcription from video remains partial. Crowd simulation looks convincing at a distance and breaks down when individuals are watched closely. Biomechanical models are useful for aggregate patterns and less reliable for any one body, and none of this replaces a dancer, a notator or a clinician.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here divide the field by what is being done to movement. Kinematic Video and Generated Movement covers synthesis from prompts and music, and is the place to start for how a phrase is produced. Dance Notation and Transcription deals with reading and writing movement in symbolic form, which matters when a generated or recorded phrase has to be preserved. Motion Capture and Retargeting explains how movement is captured from a performer and transferred to another skeleton or character, the bridge between recording and reuse. Crowd and Ensemble Simulation scales the same questions to many bodies at once, where individual accuracy gives way to group behaviour. Biomechanical Analysis closes the set by measuring movement against anatomy and physics, which is where the limits of plausibility become visible. Read together, they move from making a single phrase to preserving it, transferring it, multiplying it and testing it.
